interactions.label: Which of the following capabilities distinguishes a Level III ICU from a Level I

params.question: Which of the following capabilities distinguishes a Level III ICU from a Level II unit?

answers.text: Continuous vital-sign monitoring and basic life support

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are features of a Level I unit, the most basic tier of intensive care. Level III goes well beyond this.
These capabilities define a Level II unit. Level III adds organ-support modalities that Level II does not provide.

answers.text: Full organ support including renal replacement therapy and ECMO

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Level III units deliver the highest tier of care, including renal replacement therapy and, where available, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation — capabilities beyond what Level II units offer.

answers.text: A dedicated one-to-one nurse-to-patient ratio for all admissions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nurse-to-patient ratios are a staffing standard recommended by ISCCM (1:1 for ventilated patients), not a feature that distinguishes care levels.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three levels: Level I provides monitoring and basic support, Level II adds ventilation and invasive monitoring, and Level III adds full organ support including renal replacement therapy and ECMO.
Well done. The three-level classification reflects escalating organ-support capability, with Level III offering the most comprehensive care including RRT and ECMO.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia develops acute respiratory f

params.question: A 45-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia develops acute respiratory failure requiring intubation. His pneumonia is treatable with antibiotics, but he remains haemodynamically unstable with refractory hypotension. Under the ICU priority model, which category does this patient fall into?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. He has acute physiological instability (respiratory failure, refractory hypotension) combined with a clearly reversible underlying condition (bacterial pneumonia treatable with antibiotics). This combination defines Priority 1 — the most urgent category.

answers.text: Priority 2 — significant risk of deterioration needing close surveillance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Priority 2 is for patients who face deterioration risk but are not yet critically unstable. This patient already has established organ failure requiring active intervention, placing him above Priority 2.

answers.text: Priority 3 — condition limits the benefit of full intensive care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Priority 3 applies when the underlying condition limits the potential benefit of aggressive ICU care. This patient's pneumonia is fully treatable, so intensive care offers clear benefit.

answers.text: Priority 4 — too stable for ICU or too ill to benefit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Priority 4 covers patients who either do not need ICU-level care or whose condition is irreversible. Neither applies here — he is both critically unstable and has a treatable disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Re-examine the two axes: physiological severity and reversibility. This patient is haemodynamically unstable (high severity) with a treatable pneumonia (high reversibility) — that combination maps to Priority 1, the most urgent category.

Exactly. The priority model classifies patients on two axes — severity of physiological derangement and reversibility of the underlying condition. Unstable physiology plus a treatable cause is Priority 1.

interactions.label: Why does a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or below necessitate definitive airway

params.question: Why does a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or below necessitate definitive airway management in the unconscious patient?

answers.text: Patients below this threshold universally require immediate neurosurgical intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not all causes of low GCS are surgical. Metabolic encephalopathy, toxicological causes, and infections can all produce GCS ≤ 8 without any surgical lesion. The airway concern is independent of the aetiology.

answers.text: Below this threshold, the patient loses the ability to protect their own airway from aspiration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At GCS ≤ 8, protective reflexes such as gag and cough are impaired, placing the patient at immediate risk of aspiration. A definitive airway — typically an endotracheal tube — is required to secure the airway.

answers.text: A GCS of 8 reliably indicates brainstem herniation requiring emergency decompression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GCS ≤ 8 does not specifically indicate herniation. All four categories of unconsciousness — structural, metabolic, toxicological, and infectious — can produce this score without herniation being present.

answers.text: Mechanical ventilation can only be initiated once the GCS falls below 8

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ventilation can be initiated at any GCS level when clinically indicated. The GCS ≤ 8 threshold identifies when airway protection is lost, not when ventilation becomes technically possible.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is airway protection: at GCS ≤ 8, protective reflexes (gag, cough) are impaired and the patient can no longer guard against aspiration. That is why a definitive endotracheal tube is required.
Right. The GCS ≤ 8 threshold is fundamentally about airway protection — once protective reflexes are lost, aspiration risk mandates a definitive airway regardless of the underlying cause.

interactions.label: In volume-controlled ventilation, what happens to airway pressure if the patient

params.question: In volume-controlled ventilation, what happens to airway pressure if the patient's lung compliance suddenly decreases?

answers.text: Airway pressure falls proportionally to the compliance drop

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In VCV, tidal volume is fixed. If compliance falls, the ventilator must generate higher pressure to deliver the same volume — pressure rises, it does not fall.

answers.text: The ventilator automatically reduces tidal volume to maintain safe pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: That describes pressure-controlled ventilation, where a fixed pressure is set and tidal volume varies with compliance. In VCV, volume is the constant and pressure is the dependent variable.

answers.text: Airway pressure rises, increasing the risk of barotrauma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. VCV delivers a fixed tidal volume regardless of compliance. When compliance drops — as in ARDS — the ventilator generates higher pressures to push the same volume in, raising the risk of barotrauma.

answers.text: The respiratory rate increases automatically to compensate for reduced minute ventilation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In VCV, both tidal volume and respiratory rate are set by the clinician. The ventilator does not independently adjust rate in response to compliance changes.

overallFeedback.feedback: In VCV, tidal volume is fixed and airway pressure is the dependent variable. When compliance drops, more pressure is needed to deliver the same volume — that is why VCV carries a barotrauma risk in patients with stiff lungs.
Exactly. This is the fundamental trade-off in VCV: guaranteed minute ventilation at the cost of variable — and potentially dangerous — airway pressures when compliance worsens.

params.question: After accidental extubation in a ventilated ICU patient, a falling pulse oximetry reading is the earliest indicator of tube displacement.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. SpO₂ is a lagging indicator — residual alveolar oxygen keeps saturation normal for several minutes after tube displacement. End-tidal CO₂ drops to zero immediately, making capnography the first sign. Relying on pulse oximetry alone after extubation is a recognised patient-safety trap.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Oxygen stored in the alveoli maintains SpO₂ for several minutes after extubation. The end-tidal CO₂ waveform disappears immediately when the tube leaves the trachea, making capnography the earliest and most reliable indicator of displacement.
